'''Aewa''', also spelled '''Aiwa''' ({{lang|ash|Aʔɨwa}}), and also known as '''Abishira''', '''Tequiraca''' (Tekiráka),{{refn|Alternate spellings include ''Abigira'', ''Abijira'', ''Abira'', ''Awishiri'', ''Abixira''<ref name="clark">{{cite book |last1=Clark |first1=Patricia Roberts |title=Tribal Names of the Americas: Spelling Variants and Alternative Forms, Cross-Referenced |date=21 October 2009 |publisher=McFarland |isbn=978-0-7864-5169-2 |page=10 |language=en}}</ref> ''Avishiri'', ''Auishiri'', ''Agouisiri'', ''Avirxiri'', ''Abiquira''.}} '''Ixignor''',<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |author-link=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref> or '''Vacacocha''', is an extinct language formerly spoken in [[Peru]].  It is presumed extinct some time in the 1980s, though in 2008 two [[Speaker types#Rememberers|rememberers]] were found and 160 words and short sentences were recorded.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.cabeceras.org/cap_2010update.htm |title = Cabeceras Aid Project Winter 2010 Update |access-date= 14 April 2013}}</ref> Today, most ethnic Aiwa people have shifted to [[Kichwa language|Kichwa]] and Spanish.<ref name="Amazonian isolates 1">{{cite book |editor-last=Epps |editor-first=Patience |editor-last2=Michael |editor-first2=Lev |title=Amazonian Languages: Language Isolates. Volume I: Aikanã to Kandozi-Chapra |publisher=Walter de Gruyter |location=Berlin |date=2023 |isbn=978-3-11-041940-5}}</ref>

== Classification ==
The little data available show it to not be closely related to other languages,<ref name="Amazonian isolates 1" /> though a distant connection to [[Canichana language|Canichana]] was proposed by [[Terrence Kaufman]] (1994).<ref>{{Citation |last=Moseley|first=Christopher|title=Atlas of the world's languages|date=1994|access-date=<!--2026-05-01-->|place=London ; New York|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-01925-5|last2=Asher|first2=R. E.|last3=Tait|first3=Mary}}</ref>

== History ==
The last fluent speakers of Aʔɨwa in Puerto Elvira are thought to have died in the 1980s.<ref name="Amazonian isolates 1" /> Two people were reported to remember the language in 2008.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Crevels|first=Mily|title=The Indigenous Languages of South America|date=2012-01-13|work=|pages=167–234|editor-last=Campbell|editor-first=Lyle|url=https://amerindias.github.io/referencias/camgro12southamerica.pdf|access-date=2026-05-25|chapter=Language endangerment in South America: The clock is ticking|chapter-url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110258035.167/html|publisher=DE GRUYTER|doi=10.1515/9783110258035.167|isbn=978-3-11-025513-3|editor2-last=Grondona|editor2-first=Verónica}}</ref>

=== Language contact ===
Marcelo Jolkesky (2016) also notes that there are lexical similarities with [[Taushiro language|Taushiro]], likely as a result of prehistoric contact within the circum-Marañón interaction sphere.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016">{{cite thesis|last=Jolkesky |first=Marcelo Pinho de Valhery |date=2016 |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/tese:jolkesky-2016-arqueoecolinguistica |title=Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas |type=Ph.D. dissertation |location=Brasília |publisher=University of Brasília |edition=2}}</ref>

== Names ==
Aʔɨwa has been referred to under a variety of names in the past, among them ''Abishira''/''Awishiri'' and variants, ''Tekiraka''/''Tequiraca'', and ''Vacacocha''. In particular, ''Awishiri'' is highly ambiguous as it has been used to reference no less than four different peoples and languages: the Aʔɨwa, a subgroup of the [[Arabela people|Arabela]] people, who speak [[Arabela language|a Zaparoan language]], the [[Waorani people]], who speak [[Waorani language|a language isolate]], and an otherwise unidentified group of [[Western Tukanoan languages|Western Tukanoan]] linguistic affiliation during the colonial period. The name Aʔɨwa is the people's self-designation and the only one recognized by them. One of the consultants, Delia Andi Macahuachi, and her family members, thought the name ''Aushiri'' might refer to a group of "wild people" living on the [[Tiputini River]], possibly referring to the Waorani. [[Günter Tessmann]] (1930) records that the "civilized" Aʔɨwa objected rather strongly to being called ''Auischiri'', and the [[Sápara]], who also speak [[Záparo language|a Zaparoan language]], used the name ''Awishiri'' to refer generally to other Indigenous peoples, including the [[Chicham languages|Chicham]]-speaking [[Shuar]], other Sápara from the [[Curaray River]], and [[Napo Kichua]]. Avencio Villarejo (1959) opted for the name ''Vacacocha'' 'Cow Lake', from the name of the location the Aʔɨwa lived at the time, now part of Puerto Elvira. The name ''Tekiráka'' was first used by Tessmann (1930) as he reported it as a self-designation by the Aʔɨwa,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tessmann |first=Günther |title=Die Indianer Nordost-Perus |date=1930 |publisher=Grundlegende Forschungen für eine systematische Völkerkunde}}</ref> and has since been adopted by a number of other authors,<ref>{{Citation |last=Moseley|first=Christopher|title=Atlas of the world's languages|date=1994|access-date=<!--2026-05-01-->|place=London ; New York|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-01925-5|last2=Asher|first2=R. E.|last3=Tait|first3=Mary}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hammarström |first=Harald |date=December 2010 |title=The status of the least documented language families in the world |url=http://hdl.handle.net/10125/4478 |journal=Language Documentation and Conservation |issn=1934-5275}}</ref> although the Aʔɨwa consultants did not recognize the name as such.<ref name="Amazonian isolates 1" />{{Reference page|page=173, 175}}
